member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Audio.SoundBank
member.summary: Every sound the game can name, gathered from the directories and archives the original mounts.

remarks.para: The original mounts a sound directory with 0x4E68D0, a thin wrapper over the virtual file system's directory walk. Its per-file callback 0x4E68F0 looks at the extension and does one of two things: .WAV goes to the ILSF loader 0x495F70, and .RES is opened as an archive whose bodies are themselves sounds. Anything else is ignored.

.MP3 is the one addition, and it is the sequel's rather than an enhancement: I.G.I. 2 ships its menu theme as an MPEG stream inside menusystem/sound/sounds.res and its mission scores as loose *_music.mp3 files, where I.G.I. 1 ships IMA ADPCM for both. What decides which decoder an entry gets is its content and not its name — see — so the extension governs nothing but which loose files are worth opening.
Sounds are filed under the bare stem of their path — ak47_1, not LOCAL:common/sounds/ak47_1.wav — because that is all a script ever says. See for how the key is extracted and hashed.

First mount wins. The original's insert does not check for an existing entry, but its loader does: it looks the key up first and reports "SOUND - File %s already loaded!" without replacing anything. So a mission's own sounds cannot shadow a common one of the same name, and the mount order in Mission_Load is what decides. The port keeps that, and logs the same way.

member.summary: One entry of the sound script: the join between the name game code says and the sound the bank holds.

remarks.para: Nothing in the game names a sound file. Every call site names a definition, and the definition names the bank key. Missing that indirection makes every hook wrong in the same way — a dying guard asks for ai_death_1, which is not a bank key and never was; the definition maps it to AI_DEATH_01.

Built by DefineSound (0x4E8C60) into a SoundDefSound task of 304 bytes. The argument slots were recovered from that function's stack frame, and every one of the thirteen lands on a field: at +223, at +255, at +160, at +196, at +208, at +212, the three parameter indices at +184/+188/+192 and at +220.

DefineGraph and DefineTriggerOnce share arguments 0 to 7 with DefineSound exactly — same order, same types — and diverge only afterwards: a graph's two curves and its parameter indices, a trigger's duration, trigger index and invert flag.

member.summary: Turns a sound's file path into the name the game refers to it by, and reproduces the two hashes the original files it under.

remarks.para: A script never names a path. It says ak47_1, and the engine finds whichever file was loaded under that key from wherever it was mounted. 0x497390 is what produces the key: it finds the first dot in the path, scans back from it to the nearest /, \ or :, and copies what lies between into a 32-byte buffer. So LOCAL:common/sounds/ak47_1.wav becomes ak47_1.

The sounds are then stored in a 101-bucket hash table (0x4955F0 builds it, 0x496250 inserts, 0x496450 looks up) under two values computed by 0x497450 and 0x497410. Both upper-case as they go, so lookup is case-insensitive — and both do it in place, mutating the caller's buffer, which is why the original's key buffer comes back upper-cased.

The multiplier walk is the same family the AI graph's field names use (0x4F9E70): start at one, add a constant each character, keep it to sixteen bits. The constant differs — 317 there and in , but 318 in , which is easy to read straight past.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Resources.ResourceOverrides
member.summary: An ordered stack of folders whose files stand in for the game's own assets, addressed the way the installation addresses them.

remarks.para: Each folder mirrors the game. An asset is overridden by putting a file where that asset lives in the installation — overrides/common/textures/000_04_1.tex replaces the shared texture, overrides/missions/location0/level10/textures/000_04_1.tex replaces level 10's own, and overrides/missions/location0/level1/terrain/terrain.tex replaces a file that was already loose. Nothing has to be declared and there is no manifest: the path IS the identity.

That is what makes it able to replace an archived asset at all. Most of this game's art lives inside .res archives and is addressed by a name that is not unique — the art is layered, so common, a location and a level can each ship a different 000_04_1, and which one a level draws depends on mount order. A replacement keyed by that name could not tell them apart. A replacement keyed by WHERE THE ARCHIVE IS can, because an archive has exactly one place.

An archive in a folder works too, and means the same thing. A .res file in a layer is opened and every entry in it is registered at the path that entry would have been overridden at individually — so overrides/common/textures/textures.res holding water_igi.tex is exactly equivalent to overrides/common/textures/water_igi.tex. The archive is a delivery mechanism, not a new rule. It holds only what it replaces, so a name it does not carry resolves the way it always did.

Several layers, one rule. The layers are ordered, first highest. For every path the first ENABLED layer that has it wins; the layers below fill whatever it leaves out; a path no enabled layer has is the game's own. Within one layer a loose file beats an archived entry (someone who drops one .tex beside a generated pack is correcting that pack), and two archives that carry the same path resolve by archive path, alphabetically first, so the answer never depends on directory order.

Rescannable by design. rebuilds every layer's index and reports what moved, so a file dropped in while the game is running is picked up without a restart. An archive is INDEXED rather than loaded: the walk reads chunk headers and names and seeks past every payload, because a 4x pack's level archive is a quarter of a gigabyte and there may be fifteen of them. Switching a layer on or off () re-merges the indexes already held and touches no disk.
The bytes are read on demand and not kept here. Whoever asks holds them -- a level's resource registry, for as long as that level lives -- and lets them go with it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.TaskScriptCommands
member.summary: The script commands level data builds a task tree with: Task_New and Task_DeclareParameters.

remarks.para: A level's objects.qvm is one long sequence of these. Declarations come first, one per task type, naming every parameter and its value type; then a single deeply nested Task_New tree.

Nesting works by argument, not by block. Task_New parses its parameters, then rebinds its own symbol's context to the task it just made and evaluates its remaining arguments — so any Task_New among them attaches to that task — and finally restores the previous context. That is why parameter counts have to be exact: consume one too few and the next child becomes a parameter value; one too many and a child is silently skipped.

remarks.para: This is the mechanism that makes the original's object model work at all: update handlers routinely delete things, and a naive foreach over a child collection either throws or walks freed memory. The original keeps one global stack (0xAFA6E0, 64 slots) alongside a depth counter (0xAFA7E0) and has Task_Delete reach into it; the walk is 0x401D80.

On entry at depth d the walker writes the task it is about to message into slot d; while iterating that task's children it writes the next child still to visit into slot d+1. rewrites whichever slot names a dying task, which is what keeps both roles correct:

A task that deletes a later sibling has the parent's pending cursor advanced past it, so the loop resumes at the right place instead of following a dead link.

remarks.para: A task that deletes an earlier sibling or one of its own children needs no patch: the walk has already passed the former, and unlinking removes the latter before it is reached.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Time.ITimeSource
member.summary: The engine's only wall-clock source: a millisecond counter measured from start-up.

remarks.para: The original reads time in exactly one place, Sys_GetTickCount (0x490370), which is GetTickCount() - bias — a biased 32-bit millisecond counter with roughly 10–16 ms resolution. The single QueryPerformanceCounter call in the binary profiles texture releases and never reaches the frame schedule.

The value is a signed 32-bit integer because that is how the frame arbiter compares it: the tick deadline is truncated to 64 bits and only its low dword is compared, signed. Wrap-around behaviour therefore has to match, so widening this to 64 bits would be a behaviour change, not a cleanup.

member.summary: The real clock: milliseconds since this instance was created.

remarks.para: Reproduces Sys_GetTickCount (0x490370), which subtracts a start-up bias from GetTickCount so that the engine only ever sees time relative to launch. The returned integer keeps that signed 32-bit millisecond shape and wrap, while the backing monotonic clock has enough resolution for the remastered presentation.

The original's counter has roughly 10–16 ms resolution and the tick schedule is built around that. A higher-resolution clock is allowed — the schedule is defined by absolute deadlines rather than by measured deltas, so finer readings change only which frame notices a deadline, never the simulation — but the coarse case is the one the guards in were designed for.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Titles.GuestTitle
member.summary: One game started inside another's session, against its own installation: its own loop, file system and tables, which the host game's level borrows from.

remarks.para: A game's content declares its task types, natives and script variables into one loop's registries, and the two games name many of the same things differently (both have a HumanSoldier, with other parameters). So a guest keeps a loop of its own: its task types and natives are never mixed into the host's, its tables read its own files through its own devices, and the tasks it makes live in its own tree, ticked by whatever the host's level binds to them.

Started as the host starts a game: the installation's file system configuration applied over a device at its root, the layout's structural task types, and every content module registered before any loads its tables. Its clock runs only when the host advances it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Vfs.LocalFileDevice
member.summary: The LOCAL device: files on disk, below the installation root.

remarks.para: The original resolves LOCAL: paths against the process working directory, which is the game folder. The port takes the root explicitly so a host can point the engine at an installation anywhere, and so tests can run against a temporary directory.

Case. The game's own data was authored on a case-insensitive filesystem and its resources name each other in whatever case the author typed, so graph.res and GRAPH.RES are the same file as far as every path inside the data is concerned. That holds for free on Windows and on a default macOS volume, and not at all on Linux or on a case-sensitive APFS volume, where an installation copied from a Windows machine would half-load. The exact path is therefore tried first and a case-folded walk of the directories is the fallback, so the common case costs one File.Exists and only a genuine miss pays for a directory listing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Engine.Vfs.VirtualFileSystem
member.summary: Resolves the original engine's NAMESPACE:path names to files, through runtime-rebindable aliases over a set of named devices.

remarks.para: Resolution has exactly two stages, mirroring 0x4B1020 and 0x4B1510:

item.description: Alias substitution. The first alias whose name is a prefix of the path wins; its target replaces that prefix and the rest of the path is appended. An alias target is a semicolon-separated search list, so MISSION: can name several directories, tried in order. A path matching no alias passes through unchanged. Substitution happens once — the original does not chain aliases, and neither do we.

Device dispatch. Whatever prefix remains is a device name (LOCAL in the retail game). The device receives the path after the colon. An unknown or unregistered device is fatal, as it is in the original.

remarks.para: Aliases are bound at runtime — LANGUAGE: is rebound whenever the language changes and MISSION: whenever a mission loads — so callers must resolve at use time, never cache.
